title: Build the Network, Watch It Run
text:
Who this is for
This book is for people learning networking who want to build a topology, configure it with real Linux commands and see what happens. It is also for educators who want to author labs that grade themselves.
It assumes you can use a browser and a terminal. It does not assume you have configured a firewall before.
crumbs: Build the Network, Watch It Run

title: Build the Network, Watch It Run
text:
What NetSim is
NetSim is a network simulator that runs entirely in the browser. You drag hosts, switches, routers, firewalls and access points onto a canvas, cable them, open a terminal on any device, and use a curated subset of real iproute2, nft, iptables, DHCP, DNS and HTTP commands.
There is no backend. Topologies autosave in the browser, export as JSON, and share as compressed URLs.
crumbs: Build the Network, Watch It Run

title: Build the Network, Watch It Run
text:
What it simulates
L2 switching and VLANs, ARP, IPv4 routing with static and RIP routes, ICMP, a TCP handshake, UDP, DHCP, DNS A records, HTTP, stateful firewalling with NAT, and connection tracking. Every packet is an event you can watch.
It does not simulate IPv6, OSPF/BGP, 802.1Q trunking, TLS, real application payloads or performance. It is a teaching and design tool, not a packet-accurate emulator.
crumbs: Build the Network, Watch It Run

title: Build the Network, Watch It Run
text:
How to read it
Part 1 teaches the interface, the topology and the commands. Part 2 tests firewalls and services, and explains the bundled labs. Part 3 shows how to author, distribute and export a lab.
Each chapter ends with an AI exploration, a build or lab task, a summary and a reflection.

title: 1  A Network in the Browser
text:
1.1 The Concept First
NetSim runs entirely in the browser. It has no backend, no containers and no real kernels. It is a discrete-event simulator: devices, links and packets are objects in TypeScript, and every packet is an event on a clock.
That design gives three things a real network cannot:
The trade-off is scope. NetSim simulates a curated subset of IPv4 networking: L2 switching, ARP, static and RIP routing, ICMP, TCP handshakes, UDP, DHCP, DNS, HTTP, stateful firewalls and NAT. It does not simulate IPv6, OSPF/BGP, TLS, real payloads or performance.
It is a teaching and design tool. It is not a packet-accurate emulator.

title: 1  A Network in the Browser
text:
Determinism: the same topology and the same actions produce the same result.
Inspectability: every packet can be paused, stepped and explained.
Portability: it runs on a locked-down laptop or a Chromebook with no install.

title: 1  A Network in the Browser
text:
1.2 Understanding Through a Flight Simulator
A flight simulator does not reproduce every bolt in the aircraft. It reproduces the instruments and the decisions that matter for a flight lesson.
NetSim reproduces the decisions that matter for a networking lesson: addressing, routing, switching, firewalls and services.

title: 1  A Network in the Browser
section: 1.3 Discovering the Tool with Your AI Partner
text:
1.3 Discovering the Tool with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Separate the Model from the World
Ask the AI to list what the simulator can and cannot prove.
NetSim simulates ARP, IPv4 routing, ICMP, TCP, UDP, DHCP, DNS, HTTP,
stateful firewalls and NAT.
It does not simulate IPv6, OSPF/BGP, TLS, real payloads or performance.

For each capability, write one question the simulator can answer and one
it cannot. Do not claim the simulator proves more than its model.
A good answer keeps the model boundary visible.


Exploration 2: Find the Explainability
Ask why a deterministic simulator can explain a drop.
A real kernel drops a packet silently. A deterministic simulator can name
the rule, the interface and the exact event. Explain why that matters for
teaching and for firewall design.
The explanation is the pedagogical advantage.


Exploration 3: Choose the Use
Ask which tasks fit.
List five networking tasks. For each, say whether NetSim is a good fit,
a partial fit or the wrong tool. Include production performance testing,
firewall rule design, protocol learning and incident response.
The answer is a scope decision, not a sales pitch.

title: 2  Build a Topology
text:
2.1 The Concept First
NetSim’s device palette has six types:
Drag a device onto the canvas, or click to drop one. Cable two devices by dragging from a dot on one to a dot on the other.
Addressing can be done in two places: the Inspector fields or a terminal. Both use the same engine, so the result is identical.
The starting topology is a claim about the network. Leave unconfigured what the student must configure. Configure what the scenario provides.

title: 2  Build a Topology
text:
Host: one interface.
Server: one interface, with service editors.
Switch: eight ports, L2 forwarding and VLANs.
Router: four interfaces, IPv4 forwarding.
Firewall: four interfaces and nftables base chains.
Wi-Fi AP: a bridge with wireless client links.

title: 2  Build a Topology
text:
2.2 Understanding Through a Model Railway
A model railway is not a real railway. It is a track plan, a set of trains and a power supply that lets you test a timetable.
The topology is the track plan. The addresses and routes are the timetable.

title: 2  Build a Topology
section: 2.3 Discovering Topology with Your AI Partner

2.3 Discovering Topology with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Choose the Devices
Ask the AI to translate a scenario into devices.
Scenario: two subnets, each with two hosts, joined by a router, with a
firewall between the subnets and an internet host.

List the devices, interfaces and links. Mark which device needs a route
and which needs a firewall rule.
A good answer separates the topology from the configuration.


Exploration 2: Plan the Addressing
Ask for an address plan.
Plan IPv4 addressing for two LANs, a transit link and an internet host.
Use private ranges. For each device and interface, give the address,
prefix and default gateway.
The plan is the contract before the commands.


Exploration 3: Find the Minimum Topology
Ask what can be removed.
Here is a topology: [paste it]
Remove devices and links that do not change the question being tested.
Explain what each removal changes.
A smaller topology is easier to debug and grade.

title: 3  Configure with Real Syntax
text:
3.1 The Concept First
The terminal supports a subset of iproute2, nft, iptables, DHCP, DNS, HTTP and socket commands.
Common commands:
A firewall is a router with nftables base chains declared. Rules can be written in nft or iptables; both compile to one internal model and list in both dialects.
The important design choice: unsupported syntax produces an explicit netsim: "..." is not supported error. The tool never silently fakes a command.
That is good for learning. It also means you must read the error and check help.

title: 3  Configure with Real Syntax
text:
ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0
ip link set eth0 up
ip route add default via 192.168.1.1
ip neigh
ping 192.168.1.20
traceroute 203.0.113.10
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

title: 3  Configure with Real Syntax
text:
3.2 Understanding Through a Language Tutor
A language tutor who accepts every mistake teaches a private language. A tutor who corrects you teaches the language other people speak.
NetSim corrects you.

Intent: give pc1 the address 10.0.1.10/24 on eth0 and make 10.0.1.1 the

Exploration 2: Read the Error
Ask what an unsupported command means.

Explain what the student should do next. Do not suggest guessing.

Exploration 3: Compare Inspector and Terminal
Ask whether the two paths are equivalent.
Adding an address in the Inspector and with ip addr add both use the same
engine. Explain why that matters for teaching and for the exported
configuration.

title: 4  Follow a Packet
text:
4.1 The Concept First
A ping from pc1 to pc2 is not one event. It is a chain:
NetSim animates ARP in amber, ICMP in blue, TCP in green and UDP in purple. A red ring flashes where a firewall drops a packet.
The first ping is often slower because ARP must resolve the MAC. The second is faster because the neighbour table is warm.

title: 4  Follow a Packet
text:
The host checks whether the destination is local.
If local, it needs the destination MAC. ARP resolves it.
If remote, it sends to the default gateway and needs the gateway MAC.
The switch learns the source MAC and forwards the frame.
The router decrements TTL, checks the route and forwards.
The destination replies, and the return path repeats.

title: 4  Follow a Packet
text:
4.2 Understanding Through a Delivery Route
A parcel moves through a pickup, a depot, a flight and a local van. Each stage has a decision and a record.
A packet is the parcel. The tables are the depot records.

title: 4  Follow a Packet
section: 4.3 Discovering the Path with Your AI Partner
text:
4.3 Discovering the Path with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Predict the Path
Ask the AI to trace a packet before you run it.
pc1 192.168.1.10/24, gateway 192.168.1.1
r1 eth0 192.168.1.1/24, eth1 192.168.2.1/24
pc2 192.168.2.20/24, gateway 192.168.2.1

Predict the path of ping from pc1 to pc2. Include ARP, the switch, the
router, TTL and the return path.
The prediction makes the animation meaningful.


Exploration 2: Find the Drop
Ask how to explain a failed ping.
A ping fails. The host has an address, the link is up, and the firewall
log shows a drop. List the evidence you would collect in order and the
rule you would check.
The firewall log names the verdict. The route table shows the path.


Exploration 3: Test the First-Ping Effect
Ask why the first ping differs.
The first ping takes longer than the second. Explain why, and what you
would clear to reproduce the first-ping behaviour.
The ARP cache is the answer.

title: 5  Firewalls
text:
5.1 The Concept First
NetSim firewalls support nft and iptables front-ends over one internal rule model. A rule added in one dialect lists in both.
The model covers:
A firewall is a router with base chains declared. It also has a per-device log that names the exact rule behind every verdict.
DROP is silent. REJECT sends an ICMP unreachable or a TCP reset. The difference matters: a client sees a timeout for a drop and a refusal for a reject.

title: 5  Firewalls
text:
input, forward and output chains
accept, drop and reject verdicts
chain policies
connection tracking (ct state new,established,related)
NAT: masquerade, SNAT and DNAT port forwarding

title: 5  Firewalls
text:
5.2 Understanding Through a Nightclub Door
A door policy is an ordered list. The first matching rule decides. A broad accept at the top makes every later drop irrelevant.
A firewall is the door. The log is the bouncer’s note.

title: 5  Firewalls
section: 5.3 Discovering Firewalls with Your AI Partner
text:
5.3 Discovering Firewalls with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Write the Policy First
Ask the AI to state the policy in plain language.
A LAN may reach the internet. The internet may reach the public web
server on tcp/80 only. Everything else is dropped.

Write the firewall policy in plain language, then the nftables rules.
Do not write the rules first.
The policy is the intent. The rules are the implementation.


Exploration 2: Test DROP and REJECT
Ask how the client sees each.
Compare a silent drop and a reject for tcp/22 from the internet. What does
the client see, what does the log show and which verdict is appropriate?
A drop is quiet; a reject is a message.


Exploration 3: Read the Verdict
Ask how to explain a blocked packet.
A packet was dropped. List the evidence you would collect: chain, rule,
source, destination, protocol and state. Explain why the log is better
than guessing.
The log is the explanation.

title: 6  Services
text:
6.1 The Concept First
NetSim runs services as real packet exchanges:
All service traffic animates on the wire. Block UDP/67 and DHCP dies. Block UDP/53 and DNS dies. Block TCP/80 and the web dies.

title: 6  Services
text:
DHCP: dhclient sends DISCOVER, receives OFFER, sends REQUEST and receives ACK. The client installs the address, default route and nameserver.
DNS: an A-record server answers dig over UDP/53. Hostname resolution is wired into ping, traceroute, nc and curl.
HTTP: a configurable web server answers curl over the simulated TCP handshake.
TCP/UDP: nc tests ports, nc -l listens, ss and conntrack -L show state.

title: 6  Services
text:
6.2 Understanding Through a Postal Service
DHCP is the address assignment desk. DNS is the directory. HTTP is the parcel.
Each has a protocol, a server and a failure mode.

title: 6  Services
section: 6.3 Discovering Services with Your AI Partner
text:
6.3 Discovering Services with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Trace DHCP
Ask the AI to label the four packets.
dhclient runs on pc2 against a DHCP server. List the four packets, the
direction, the transport and what the client installs after the ACK.
A good answer names DISCOVER, OFFER, REQUEST and ACK.


Exploration 2: Break DNS
Ask what happens when UDP/53 is blocked.
A firewall drops udp/53 between pc2 and the DNS server. Explain what
happens to dig, ping by name and curl by name. What still works by IP?
The failure is specific, not “the network is down”.


Exploration 3: Test the Web
Ask how to read a curl failure.
curl http://web.lan/ fails. List the checks in order: DNS, route, TCP
connect, firewall and server. Explain what each result would tell you.
A structured diagnosis beats guessing.

title: 7  Labs and Auto-Grading
text:
7.1 The Concept First
NetSim ships five guided labs:
Each lab has steps, objectives and quizzes. The Check objectives button runs the checks against the live simulation using real packets. Students see the grader’s probes animate.
The checks are passive or active. Passive checks read device state, such as an interface address or a firewall policy. Active checks send packets, such as a ping, a TCP connect, a DNS query or an HTTP fetch.
A lab is not a quiz with a network attached. It is a scenario with evidence.

title: 7  Labs and Auto-Grading
text:
Static addressing and ARP
Routing between networks
Build a stateful firewall
DHCP, DNS and the web
Harden a vulnerable network

title: 7  Labs and Auto-Grading
text:
7.2 Understanding Through a Driving Test
A driving test does not ask whether you read the manual. It watches you drive.
A NetSim lab watches the packets.

title: 7  Labs and Auto-Grading
section: 7.3 Discovering the Labs with Your AI Partner
text:
7.3 Discovering the Labs with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Map Lab to Concept
Ask the AI to match each lab to a concept.
Here are the five NetSim labs:
[paste them]

For each, name the main concept and one check that proves it. Explain
why a passive check is not enough on its own.
Active checks prove behaviour; passive checks prove configuration.


Exploration 2: Prove the Problem
Ask why a security lab checks the vulnerability first.
Lab 5 asks students to confirm the exposure before they harden it.
Explain why this is better than starting with the fix. What does it
teach about evidence?
The first objective establishes the current state.


Exploration 3: Choose the Verdict
Ask about filtered versus refused.
A firewall drops tcp/22 silently. Another rejects it. Which check should
a hardening lab use, and what does the student learn from the difference?
A silent drop is usually the stronger security outcome.

Auto-grading gives immediate feedback. It is formative, not a proctored exam. The attempt file is editable, so use it for learning and evidence, not high-stakes assessment.

title: 8  Design a Lab That Checks the Right Thing
text:
8.1 The Concept First
A NetSim objective has an id, a student-facing label and a check. The check is passive or active.
Common check types:
The design question is not “what did I teach?” It is “what evidence would prove the student did it?”
crumbs: 8  Design a Lab That Checks the Right Thing

title: 8  Design a Lab That Checks the Right Thing
text:
iface-ip: an interface has an address or an address in a subnet.
default-route: a default route exists, optionally via a gateway.
forwarding: IP forwarding matches the expected value.
fw-policy: a chain policy matches.
ping: an ICMP echo succeeds or fails.
tcp: a TCP connect is open, refused or filtered.
dns: a name resolves or returns NXDOMAIN.
http: a GET succeeds, optionally with a required string.
crumbs: 8  Design a Lab That Checks the Right Thing

title: 8  Design a Lab That Checks the Right Thing
text:
8.2 Understanding Through a Building Inspection
An inspector does not ask whether the builder read the code. The inspector checks the exit, the alarm and the record.
A lab objective is the check. The step is the instruction.
crumbs: 8  Design a Lab That Checks the Right Thing

title: 8  Design a Lab That Checks the Right Thing
section: 8.3 Discovering Objectives with Your AI Partner
text:
8.3 Discovering Objectives with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Turn a Step into a Check
Ask the AI to choose a check.
Step: "Give pc1 the address 192.168.1.10/24 on eth0."
Write the objective and the check. Then write a second objective that
proves the host can reach its gateway.
One check for configuration, one for behaviour.


Exploration 2: Prove the Problem
Ask for a vulnerability-first objective.
A lab asks students to harden a network. Write an objective that passes
while the vulnerability exists, then the objective that passes after the
fix. Explain the order.
The first objective establishes the baseline.


Exploration 3: Find the Weak Check
Ask what a check misses.
A lab checks that tcp/22 is filtered from the internet. What does that
not prove? Write a second check that closes the gap.
A check is evidence for one claim, not all claims.

9.1 The Concept First
A NetSim lab file has the same shape as a topology, plus a top-level lab object:
A step has a title, a body, objectives and an optional quiz. A quiz answer is a zero-based index.
The recommended authoring path:

section: 9.3 Discovering the Format with Your AI Partner
text:
9.3 Discovering the Format with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Build the Skeleton
Ask the AI to draft the JSON.
Write a NetSim lab skeleton for a two-host addressing lab. Include the
lab id, title, blurb, one step with a title, body, two objectives and
one quiz question. Use JSON, not prose.
A skeleton is easier to review than a blank file.


Exploration 2: Test the Check
Ask what could go wrong.
A lab objective uses `iface-ip` with `inSubnet`. List the ways it could
pass without the student understanding subnetting. Write a stronger
second check.
A check is not a lesson.


Exploration 3: Plan Distribution
Ask how to hand it out.
Compare distributing a lab as a JSON file, a share link and a bundled
lab in the repository. Include the trade-offs for updating, versioning
and collecting attempts.
Each route has a maintenance cost.

title: 10  Export to the Real World
text:
10.1 The Concept First
NetSim exports more than a picture:
The generated configs are validated in CI against the real nft and dnsmasq binaries. That is the bridge from the simulator to a real machine.
The export is not a promise that the real network will behave identically. It is a starting point that preserves the design.
crumbs: 10  Export to the Real World

title: 10  Export to the Real World
text:
Device config bundle (.zip): per-device setup.sh, nftables.conf and dnsmasq.conf.
Containerlab topology: a .clab.yml with Linux nodes and firewall rules.
Docker Compose: an approximate L2 topology.
SVG/PNG diagrams: documentation-grade topology images.
Printable HTML report: diagram, inventory, cabling, routing tables, DHCP/DNS and firewall rulesets.
crumbs: 10  Export to the Real World

title: 10  Export to the Real World
text:
10.2 Understanding Through a Building Plan
A building plan is not the building. It is the document a builder can follow.
The export is the plan. The real network is the building.

title: 10  Export to the Real World
section: 10.3 Discovering Exports with Your AI Partner
text:
10.3 Discovering Exports with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Choose the Export
Ask which export fits the task.
A team wants to hand a firewall design to an engineer, run it in a lab,
and include it in a report. Which NetSim exports fit each task? Explain
the limits.
Different artefacts for different readers.


Exploration 2: Review the Config
Ask what to check before running it.
Here is a generated nftables.conf:
[paste it]

List the checks before applying it to a real host: interfaces, addresses,
default policy, rule order, NAT and rollback.
A generated config is a draft until reviewed.


Exploration 3: Compare Simulation and Reality
Ask what changes.
The simulated network works. The real containerlab deployment does not.
List the differences that could explain it: interface names, kernel
settings, L2 behaviour, image versions and timing.
The export removes typing, not thinking.

title: Appendix A — Lab Map
text: A.1 Example networks

title: Appendix A — Lab Map
text:
Segmented network: LAN and DMZ behind a stateful firewall, masquerade outbound, tcp/80 DNAT to the DMZ web server.
Flat open network: one segment, exposed services, no rules. Use it to find every problem or as the starting point for a hardening exercise.

title: Appendix A — Lab Map
text:
A.2 Suggested teaching route

Lab 1: addressing and ARP.
Lab 2: routing.
Lab 4: services.
Lab 3: firewall.
Lab 5: hardening.

The order can vary. The concepts build from local delivery to policy.

title: Appendix B — Check Types
text: B.1 Design tips

title: Appendix B — Check Types
text:
Keep objective IDs stable; saved progress is keyed by ID.
Use passive checks for configuration and active checks for behaviour.
Prove the problem before the fix in security labs.
Use filtered for a silent drop and refused for a reset or unreachable.
Order active checks by the story you want the grader’s packets to tell.
Treat auto-grading as formative feedback, not a proctored exam.

title: Acknowledgments
text:
This book is a companion to NetSim, a browser-based network simulator and firewall teaching tool. NetSim is a modern successor to the iNetwork Simulator built at the University of Technology Sydney, described in Ye and Sandrasegaran’s 2006 IEEE paper on teaching firewall concepts.
NetSim uses a curated subset of real Linux syntax and errors loudly on anything outside it. That design choice shapes this book: the commands are meant to travel to a real machine within the documented subset.

title: About the Author
text:
Michael Borck is a software developer and educator working at the intersection of human expertise and artificial intelligence. He teaches networking, security, applied AI and systems analysis, and builds browser-based tools for learning.
His books include Follow the Packet, Break with Permission, Assume Breach, Build It, Teach It and The Great Silence.
Build the Network, Watch It Run is the field guide to NetSim: build the network, watch the packet, explain the verdict.
